Full House

A row, column or box that has only one empty cell left can only be missing one digit, and that digit has to go in that cell. No candidate work is needed at all, you just read off which digit the unit does not have yet.
Look for any unit that is eight cells full and one cell empty. Scanning for almost complete boxes after every few placements is the quickest way to find them.
Last Digit

When a digit has been placed in every box but one, there is only one cell left in the whole grid that can still take it. The count alone forces the placement, so you do not have to look at candidates.
Pick a digit and count how often it already appears. At eight out of nine, find the box that is missing it and look for the single cell in that box the digit can still reach.
Naked Single
A cell whose row, column and box between them already show every digit but one has only that digit left, so it must hold it. This is the most direct deduction in the game.
Look for cells with only one pencil mark left. Without pencil marks, check cells sitting where a full row and a full column cross, they run out of options first.
Hidden Single in a Box

A digit has to appear once in every box. If everything else in the box is blocked by the same digit in a crossing row or column, the one cell left over must hold it, even if that cell still has other pencil marks.
Take one digit and one box. Cross out every cell of the box that shares a row or column with that digit elsewhere. If exactly one cell survives, that is the placement.
Hidden Single in a Line

The same argument as in a box, made along a row or a column: if a digit can only go in one cell of that line, it goes there. It is harder to see because a line is spread across the grid rather than sitting in one square block.
Walk one row at a time and ask, for a single digit, which of its empty cells could still take it. Only one candidate cell means a placement.
Pointing Pair

If every place a digit could still go inside a box lies on one row or one column, then that digit is definitely somewhere on that line inside the box. It can therefore be removed from the rest of the line outside the box.
Look at one digit inside one box. If its two or three remaining cells all share a row or a column, look along that line outside the box and clear the digit there.
Claiming

The mirror image of the pointing pair: if every place a digit could go on a row or column lies inside a single box, the digit belongs to that box on that line, so it can be removed from the rest of the box.
Take one digit and one line. If all of its candidate cells on that line fall inside one box, clear the digit from the other cells of that box.
Naked Pair

Two cells of the same unit that both hold exactly the same two candidates will use up both of those digits between them, whichever way round they fall. No other cell of that unit can take either digit.
Scan a unit for two cells with exactly two pencil marks each, and check whether the two marks are identical. Then clear those two digits from the rest of the unit.
Hidden Pair
If two digits can only go in the same two cells of a unit, those two cells are reserved for them. Every other pencil mark in those two cells can go, even though the pair was hidden behind them.
Count, for each digit of a unit, how many cells could take it. Two digits with the same two candidate cells are a hidden pair. Clean the two cells out down to just those digits.
Naked Triple

Three cells of a unit that between them use only three different candidates must hold those three digits. The digits are used up, so no other cell of the unit can take any of them. A cell may hold only two of the three, that still counts.
Look for a group of three cells in one unit whose pencil marks together add up to just three different digits, then clear those digits from the rest of the unit.
Hidden Triple
Three digits that can only be placed in the same three cells of a unit own those cells. Any other candidate in those three cells can be removed, which is what usually breaks the position open.
For each digit in a unit, note its candidate cells. Three digits whose candidate cells together cover only three cells are a hidden triple.
X-Wing

Take one digit and two rows in which it can only go in the same two columns. Whichever way the digit falls in those rows, both of those columns get it inside the rectangle, so the digit cannot appear anywhere else in those two columns.
Pick a digit and look for two rows where it has exactly two candidate cells that line up in the same two columns. The four cells form a rectangle. It works with rows and columns swapped as well.
Skyscraper
Two rows in which a digit has exactly two candidate cells, sharing one column, form a chain: one of the two far ends must hold the digit. Any cell that sees both far ends can therefore lose it.
Find two rows where a digit has just two candidates each, with one candidate of each in the same column. Then look at the two remaining ends and at the cells that see both.
Two-String Kite

A row and a column in which a digit has only two candidate cells, with one end of each meeting in the same box, chain together. One of the two far ends holds the digit, so the cell that sees both loses it.
Look for a row pair and a column pair of one digit whose near ends land in a common box. The elimination sits where the far row cell and the far column cell cross.
Swordfish

The X-Wing idea one size larger: three rows in which a digit is confined to the same three columns lock the digit into those columns, so it can be cleared from them everywhere else. A row may use only two of the three columns.
Pick a digit and look for three rows whose candidate cells for it fall within a set of just three columns, then clear the digit from those columns in every other row.
BUG+1

If every unsolved cell but one has exactly two candidates, the grid is one step away from a position with two solutions, which a proper puzzle cannot have. The cell with the extra candidate has to take that extra digit to prevent it.
Late in a puzzle, check whether all remaining cells have two pencil marks except a single cell with three. The odd digit out in that cell is the answer.
Crane

A relative of the skyscraper: two rows where the digit has two candidates each, and a third line linking them, so that one of the two far ends must hold the digit. Cells that see both ends can lose it.
Look for the skyscraper shape but with the two strong lines joined through a third line rather than sharing a box.
XY-Wing

Three cells with two candidates each: a pivot holding X and Y, one wing holding X and Z, another holding Y and Z, both seen by the pivot. Whichever digit the pivot takes, one wing ends up as Z, so any cell seeing both wings cannot be Z.
Hunt for a two-candidate cell that sees two other two-candidate cells sharing one digit with it each and a third digit with each other. The elimination is where the two wings both look.
Unique Rectangle Type 1

Four cells forming a rectangle across two boxes, holding the same two digits, would give the puzzle two solutions. Since a proper puzzle has exactly one, the fourth cell must take one of its extra candidates, so the two shared digits can go from it.
Look for three cells of a rectangle with the identical two pencil marks and a fourth corner holding those two plus extras. The two shared digits leave the fourth corner.
Unique Rectangle Type 2

The same deadly rectangle, but with one extra candidate appearing in two of the corners. That extra digit has to be placed in one of them, otherwise the puzzle would have two solutions, so every cell seeing both corners loses it.
Find a rectangle of two digits where two corners carry one and the same extra candidate. Clear that extra digit from the cells both corners see.
XYZ-Wing
Like the XY-Wing but the pivot holds three candidates, X, Y and Z, and both wings hold Z. One of the three cells has to be Z, so any cell seeing all three of them cannot be Z.
Find a three-candidate pivot with two two-candidate wings it sees, all three sharing one common digit. The elimination has to see the pivot and both wings.
W-Wing

Two cells far apart holding the same two candidates, joined by a line on which one of those digits has only two places. That link forces one of the two cells to take the other digit, so cells seeing both lose it.
Look for two identical two-candidate cells, then check whether one of their digits has a two-cell line linking them.
Finned X-Wing
An X-Wing spoiled by one extra candidate, the fin, sitting in the same box as one corner. The conclusion still holds, but only for the cells that also see the fin.
Find an almost X-Wing where one row has a third candidate. If that extra cell shares a box with a corner, you can still eliminate inside that box.
Naked Quad
Four cells of a unit using only four different candidates between them take those four digits, so no other cell of the unit can hold any of them. Cells with two or three of the four still count.
Look for four cells in one unit whose pencil marks together make up only four digits. It is easiest when at least two of them have just two marks.
Hidden Quad
Four digits restricted to the same four cells of a unit own those cells, so every other candidate in them can be removed. It is rare, and usually easier to spot as the naked subset it leaves behind.
For each digit of a unit, list its candidate cells. Four digits whose cells cover only four positions form the quad.
Unique Rectangle Type 3

A deadly rectangle where two corners carry extra candidates. Those extras behave like a small naked subset together with another cell of the unit, so that subset\'s digits can be cleared from the rest of the unit.
Find the rectangle, take the extra candidates of the two roof cells as a set, and look for cells in the same unit that complete it into a naked pair or triple.
Unique Rectangle Type 4
A deadly rectangle in which one of the two shared digits is locked into the roof line. That forces the other shared digit out of both roof cells, since otherwise the ambiguous rectangle would appear.
Find a rectangle of two digits and check whether one of them can only go in the two roof cells of its line. Then remove the other digit from those roof cells.
Empty Rectangle

A digit inside a box that occupies only one row and one column forms a cross. Combined with a two-cell line of the same digit elsewhere, it forces the digit out of the cell where the two arguments meet.
Look for a box where a digit\'s candidates all sit on one row and one column, then find a line with exactly two candidates of the digit pointing into it.
Finned Swordfish
A swordfish with one extra candidate spoiling it. The eliminations still stand, but only in the box that the fin sits in.
Find an almost swordfish where one line has a spare candidate, and check whether that spare shares a box with the cells you wanted to eliminate.
Sashimi Swordfish
A finned swordfish missing one of its corners. The pattern looks incomplete, but the argument through the fin works exactly the same way.
As the finned swordfish, except that one of the base lines has only a single candidate left inside the cover columns.
Jellyfish
The fish one size larger again: four rows in which a digit is confined to the same four columns lock it into those columns, so it can be cleared from them in every other row.
Pick a digit and look for four rows whose candidates all fall inside a set of four columns. Anything smaller is a swordfish or an X-Wing.
Simple Colouring

Follow one digit through the lines where it has exactly two places, painting the two ends in alternating colours. If a colour appears twice in one unit it is wrong, so the other colour is true. Cells that see both colours lose the digit.
Pick a digit, find its two-candidate lines and colour the chain. Then look for a colour repeating in a unit, or for cells seeing both colours.
WXYZ-Wing
The wing family extended to four cells and four candidates. One shared digit has to end up in the group, so cells that see every cell holding that digit can lose it.
Look for four cells within two units whose candidates total four digits, one of which appears in all the cells that a target cell sees.
X-Chain

A chain in a single digit, alternating between links that must be true and links that must be false. If both ends of the chain cannot be false at the same time, any cell seeing both ends loses the digit.
Follow one digit through lines where it has only two places, then check the cells that see both ends of the chain.
XY-Chain
A chain of two-candidate cells, each sharing a digit with the next. If both ends can offer the same digit, any cell seeing both ends cannot hold it.
Start from a two-candidate cell and step to a peer that shares one of its digits, continuing until an end offers the digit you started from.
Alternating Inference Chain

A chain that alternates between strong links, where at least one end is true, and weak links, where at most one end is true. Whatever the chain\'s two ends are, one of them is true, which rules the digit out of anything seeing both.
Build a chain that alternates strong and weak links across any digits, then check what both ends of it see.
ALS-XZ

Two groups of cells that are one digit short of being locked, sharing a digit that can only be in one of the two groups. That link forces a second shared digit into one of them, so cells seeing all of its places lose it.
Find two almost locked sets, check that one common digit can only sit in one of them, then eliminate the other common digit where both sets can see.
Sue de Coq

Where a box and a line cross, the shared cells can sometimes be split into two locked sets, one belonging to the line and one to the box. Both the rest of the line and the rest of the box then lose those digits.
Look at the two or three cells a box and a line share, and check whether their candidates split cleanly into a set the line covers and a set the box covers.
3D Medusa

Simple colouring done over all digits at once, colouring candidates rather than cells. The same contradictions apply, and they turn up far more often because the chain can hop between digits inside a cell.
Colour a candidate, then colour everything forced by it: the other candidate of a two-candidate cell, and the other end of a two-place line. Look for a colour twice in one unit.
Grouped Chain
An alternating chain whose links may be whole groups of candidates in a box rather than single cells. Treating a group as one node reaches conclusions no single-cell chain can.
Build a chain as usual, but allow a node to be all the candidates of a digit inside one box row or box column.
ALS Chain

Several almost locked sets joined one after another, each pair sharing a digit that can only be in one of them. The chain behaves like one long argument, and its two ends share a digit that can then be eliminated.
Chain almost locked sets by restricted common digits, then eliminate the digit both ends share from the cells all of its places can see.
